analysis.one_liner: Bans drug companies from paying generic and biosimilar makers to delay cheaper competition.
analysis.headline: The Senate Judiciary Committee approved the bill with bipartisan support in April 2025 and placed it on the Senate calendar, but the full Senate has not voted on it.
analysis.plain_summary: When a brand-name drug company is sued by a generic maker over patents, the two sometimes settle by having the brand company pay the generic maker to stay off the market for years — a "pay-for-delay" deal. This bill makes those deals illegal. It lets the Federal Trade Commission sue companies that make such agreements, with fines of up to three times the value transferred, and it strips a generic maker of its 180-day head start on the market if it signs one. It also requires drug company executives to certify under penalty that the full agreement, including any side deals or oral promises, has been filed with the FTC and the Justice Department.
analysis.who_benefits: Patients and taxpayers who pay for prescription drugs. Generic drugs cost 80 to 85 percent less than brand-name versions on average, so ending pay-for-delay deals means cheaper versions reach the market sooner. Because federal programs like Medicare cover over 40 percent of the roughly $450 billion spent on retail prescription drugs each year, taxpayers share directly in the savings. Generic and biosimilar manufacturers also benefit from entering markets earlier, even though they lose the option of being paid to wait.

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits any agreement settling a drug patent claim that has anticompetitive effects, and presumes an agreement is anticompetitive when the generic or biosimilar filer receives something of value and agrees to delay its own sales.
Lets the FTC bring civil actions and impose penalties of up to three times the value transferred, and strips a violating generic maker of its 180-day marketing exclusivity period.

Requires the CEO or negotiating official to certify to the FTC and Justice Department that the filed materials are the complete agreement, including related side agreements and any oral promises, closing a common loophole.

The bill's findings state that generic drugs cost 80 to 85 percent less than brand-name versions, and that biological drugs — already more than half of all prescription drug spending — face the same pay-for-delay threat.

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name drug manufacturers, whose profits currently depend partly on extending monopoly periods by paying potential competitors to wait, and generic or biosimilar makers that have accepted such payments. Legitimate settlements are protected: deals where the generic gets only an earlier launch date, payment of litigation costs up to $7.5 million a year, or a promise not to sue remain allowed.

drawbacks.text: Some settlements that include payment are genuinely procompetitive — for example, paying a generic maker to manufacture the drug or to supply it at a guaranteed price. The bill responds by allowing such deals if the parties prove the value is compensation for real goods or services, or that the deal's procompetitive benefits outweigh the harm, but that proof standard still invites litigation and could chill some legitimate settlements.

The bill requires the FTC to study whether to add an exclusion for settlements that release damage claims, acknowledging that the boundary between a legitimate release and disguised payment is not fully settled.

An honest supporter would acknowledge that not every delayed generic entry traces to a pay-for-delay deal, so the law will not by itself fix drug prices, and enforcement depends on FTC resources and priorities.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit is large and well-documented: courts and the FTC have treated pay-for-delay deals as a straightforward transfer of monopoly profits shared between the brand and the generic at consumers' expense, and the carve-outs in the bill protect the legitimate kinds of settlements. The main cost is legal friction — companies will litigate over whether a payment was for services or for delay — but the exclusions, the litigation-expense cap, and the FTC study provision show the drafters tried to design around that problem. On balance the bill's benefits to drug payers clearly outweigh its drawbacks.

outcome.mechanism: The bill cleared the Senate Judiciary Committee on a bipartisan basis and was placed on the Senate calendar in April 2025, where it is waiting for the full Senate to take it up.

narrative.text: Senator Klobuchar introduced the bill on March 24, 2025, joined by Senator Grassley and seven other senators from both parties, and it was referred to the Judiciary Committee.
The Judiciary Committee ordered the bill reported favorably with an amendment in the nature of a substitute on April 3, 2025, and it was reported on April 10, 2025.
The bill was placed on the Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders as Calendar No. 46, meaning it is waiting for floor time, and no floor vote has been scheduled.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Brand-name drug makers, who so far keep the ability to settle patent suits by paying generic and biosimilar rivals to delay entry, with no new penalties applying.

for.name: Sen. Amy Klobuchar
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and assembled a bipartisan group of nine original senators behind it.

for.name: Sen. Chuck Grassley
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill and reported it out of the Judiciary Committee with an amendment on April 10, 2025.

for.name: Senators Durbin, Blumenthal, Welch, Kelly, and Booker
for.what_they_did: Signed on as original cosponsors, giving the bill a bipartisan bloc in committee.

for.name: Senators Cramer and Ernst
for.what_they_did: Signed on as original cosponsors from the Republican side.

against.name: Brand-name pharmaceutical industry
against.what_they_did: Opposed versions of this pay-for-delay ban in prior Congresses; the industry has a long record of fighting legislation restricting such settlements.

sides.party_line_note: The nine original sponsors split 5 Democrats and 3 Republicans plus the Democratic lead sponsor, and the bill was reported from the Judiciary Committee by a Republican senator, though no floor vote has tested the full chamber's split.

industries.note: The bill removes their ability to settle patent suits by paying generic and biosimilar rivals to stay off the market, which protects years of monopoly pricing. Patients pay more during those delays, so the industry's interest runs directly against consumers here.

They lose the option of being paid to delay entry, but they gain earlier access to markets they would otherwise be paid to stay out of, and the bill preserves their right to sue under the antitrust laws. Their interest in faster entry matches what patients want.

industries.industry: Federal taxpayers and public drug programs
industries.note: Federal dollars cover over 40 percent of the roughly $450 billion spent annually on retail prescription drugs, so faster generic and biosimilar entry lowers the government's drug bill directly.

analysis.trajectory: The bill has cleared committee with bipartisan support and is on the Senate calendar, but bills at this stage often sit indefinitely waiting for floor time. Versions of this pay-for-delay ban have been introduced in prior Congresses with similar bipartisan backing and never received a Senate vote. Its most realistic paths are a Senate floor vote if leadership makes time, or attachment of its provisions to a larger drug-pricing or health bill.
